def: The expected loss of a model on new cases drawn from the same distribution as its training data, which can only be estimated, never observed directly.
The difference between a model's error on unseen data and its error on the data it was trained on.
Fitting the quirks and noise of the training sample so closely that error on new data is much higher than error on training data.
Using a model too rigid to capture the real pattern, so error is high on both training and new data.
How rich a family of functions a learning algorithm can choose from, such as polynomial degree or tree depth.
The part of the labelled data used to fit a model's parameters.
The held-out part of the labelled data used to compare candidates and choose hyperparameters.
Held-out data used once, after all choices are made, to report an honest estimate of generalisation error.
A setting chosen by the practitioner rather than learned from data, such as polynomial degree or learning rate.
The part of the error caused by noise in the labels that no model could predict, setting a floor on achievable error.
The optimism that comes from reporting the best score among many noisy candidates on the same data.
Independent and identically distributed: each example is drawn separately from the same distribution, an assumption behind most validation methods.
The assumptions built into a learning algorithm that let it prefer some functions over others when the data alone cannot decide.
The result that, averaged over all possible target functions, every learning algorithm has the same accuracy on unseen inputs.
